passage:
Siddharth,
I'm writing this instead of saying it in the mess, because I don't want an audience.
Last night at Rohan's birthday, Kunal did that joke about the canteen uncle's accent. Everyone laughed, and so did you. In first year you were the one who walked out when someone mocked how the laundry aunty spoke. You told me that kind of joke made your skin crawl.
Maybe you've changed your mind, and that's allowed. Maybe you're just tired of being the odd one out in the new group. I saw the others glance at you, and Kunal started on "Siddharth's new sense of humour." I didn't join in, and I won't.
If something's going on, I'd like to hear it, over chai at the gate stall, whenever you want. If nothing is, tell me I'm overthinking and I'll drop it.
Still your friend,
Harish

qa.q: Where does Harish suggest meeting Siddharth to talk?
qa.a: Over chai at the gate stall, whenever Siddharth wants.

qa.q: What is Harish feeling while writing this letter?
qa.a: Harish seems uneasy and a little sad to see Siddharth laugh at a joke Siddharth once walked out over, but also caring, not angry.

qa.q: Why was a private letter wiser than joining Kunal's teasing?
qa.a: It lets Siddharth explain, or say nothing is wrong, without the group watching, so the friendship stays safe either way.

qa.q: How might Siddharth feel reading this compared with hearing the teasing at the party?
qa.a: Siddharth may feel relieved and less cornered by a quiet letter, though perhaps a little embarrassed that the change was noticed.

grounding: Illustrates a friend who notices someone laughing along with jokes they used to dislike and reaches out privately and kindly instead of teasing in front of the group.

passage:
Himani,
You asked why I never make it to Thursday badminton anymore. Honest answer: I finish my reports by six, and then I sit at my desk until almost nine, pretending to reread them.
Nobody told me to. Farhan, our team lead, stays. Nisha and Arjun stay. The lights stay on. The one evening I packed up at six-thirty, Arjun said "Half day?" with a grin, and I replayed it the whole ride home.
I keep thinking that if I'm the first to leave, they'll decide I'm not serious about the job. The strange part is that nobody seems to do much after seven. Farhan scrolls on his phone, Nisha orders snacks, Arjun watches cricket clips with the sound off.
I've never once asked whether any of us actually needs to be there. Maybe I should.
Save me a court next Thursday? I'll try.
Lalit

qa.q: By what time does Lalit finish the reports?
qa.a: Lalit finishes the reports by six.

qa.q: What worry keeps Lalit at the desk until almost nine?
qa.a: Lalit is anxious that leaving first will make the team think Lalit is not serious, a fear sharpened by Arjun's "Half day?" joke.

qa.q: What small step could Lalit try to test whether staying late is really needed?
qa.a: Lalit could ask Farhan plainly what is expected once the work is done, or leave at six on a finished day and notice what actually happens.

qa.q: How might Himani see Lalit's missed badminton evenings after reading this?
qa.a: Himani may feel a bit let down at first, then realise Lalit is stuck in a habit driven by worry, not by work.

grounding: Illustrates a young professional who stays late only because the whole team does, fearing looking uncommitted and never questioning whether the habit helps anyone.

Note for Dolma's three-month review, from the floor supervisor.
Dolma has settled into the accounts team well. She follows the team's small customs without fuss: she joins the Monday tea round, remembered Lokesh's birthday with a card, and keeps the shared printer tidy.
On Thursday I saw something else. At lunch, Kavya and Lokesh started on the new trainee's "attitude" and turned to Dolma for agreement. Dolma said, "I haven't worked with her enough to say. Has anyone asked her?" and went back to her rice. No lecture, no sulking. Kavya looked put out; Lokesh changed the subject. Dolma still sat with them the next day.
What I did next: in our one-to-one I told Dolma I had noticed and asked whether she felt pressured. She said, "A bit. But I'd rather be the boring one at lunch." I will keep an ear on how the trainee is talked about.

qa.q: What did Dolma say when Kavya and Lokesh wanted agreement about the trainee?
qa.a: Dolma said, "I haven't worked with her enough to say. Has anyone asked her?"

qa.q: How did Dolma feel about stepping out of the lunch gossip?
qa.a: Dolma felt a little pressured and uncomfortable, yet calm and settled about the choice, as "I'd rather be the boring one at lunch" shows.

qa.q: What does Dolma's approach get right about group customs?
qa.a: Dolma keeps the kind customs like the tea round and the birthday card, declines only the gossip, and does it without preaching or leaving the group.

qa.q: How might Kavya have experienced Dolma's reply?
qa.a: Kavya may have felt awkward and a bit checked, since the easy agreement did not come, but nobody was attacked, so the table could carry on.

grounding: Shows a young adult who keeps courteous team customs, politely declines gossip, and dissents calmly without condemning the group.

In the courtyard, two-year-old Tanuja toddled toward the buffalo's water trough. Amma called, "No, no, Tanu!" but she was laughing, so Tanuja kept going and splashed.
Then Irfan, the neighbour, set a kettle of hot tea on the low step. Amma's face went still. "Tanu. Come here," she said quietly.
Tanuja stopped, stared at Amma's face, and walked straight back to her lap. The older cousins stopped giggling too.

qa.q: What did Irfan set on the low step?
qa.a: Irfan set a kettle of hot tea on the low step.

qa.q: Why did Tanuja stop the second time, even though Amma spoke quietly?
qa.a: Amma's still face and serious tone made Tanuja feel unsure and a little worried, so the feeling behind the words mattered more than the words.

qa.q: What could Amma do so her words and face match next time?
qa.a: When something really matters, Amma could say "no" with a calm, serious face from the start instead of laughing.

qa.q: What is it like for Amma to see Tanuja ignore "No, no" but obey a quiet call?
qa.a: Amma may feel relieved, and may also notice that her laughing "No, no" told Tanuja it was a game.

grounding: Shows a toddler stopping or carrying on according to the caregiver's face and tone rather than the words.

Note, KG-B, Tuesday.
Clean-up time was loud. Zubin and two others kept building. When our helper, Mrs Rao, snapped "Stop NOW," Mahima dropped her blocks at once and stood stiffly by the shelf, first to finish. Mrs Rao praised her, but Mahima did not smile. She kept glancing at Mrs Rao and twisting her pinafore.
Later she whispered to me, "Is Rao ma'am angry?" I sat beside her and said nobody was cross with her. I will suggest a calm clap-song signal for clean-up, and mention it to her parents at pickup.

qa.q: Who snapped "Stop NOW" at clean-up time?
qa.a: Mrs Rao, the helper, snapped "Stop NOW."

qa.q: What does Mahima's twisting of her pinafore suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Mahima felt anxious and scared of disapproval, not proud, even though she looked like the best-behaved child.

qa.q: Why is a calm clap-song signal a better idea for clean-up?
qa.a: It gets the children moving without fear, so tidying comes from the routine rather than from worry about an angry voice.

qa.q: How might Mrs Rao see Mahima's quick tidying?
qa.a: Mrs Rao probably sees it as good discipline and feels pleased, without noticing the worry behind it.

grounding: Shows a young child who obeys instantly when an adult's voice turns sharp, looking well-disciplined while actually anxious.

"Ritu, put that book back. Sir said nobody touches the class library without asking me."
"I'm returning it, Pankaj."
"Still. Sir said."
Thomas looked up from his drawing. "And why can't Meena come out for the game?"
"Sir said anyone who forgot homework stays in at break."
"But her pencil box got stolen yesterday. That's why she couldn't do it."
Pankaj frowned. "Sir is Sir. He knows."
"Does he know about the pencil box?"
"...I don't know." Pankaj glanced at Meena, sitting alone with her head on the desk. "He said it, so it's the rule."
Ritu slid the book onto the shelf anyway. "The book rule is about books. This one's about a person."
Pankaj twisted the monitor badge on his shirt and said nothing.

qa.q: Why couldn't Meena do her homework, according to Thomas?
qa.a: Her pencil box got stolen yesterday.

qa.q: What does Pankaj twisting the monitor badge suggest?
qa.a: Pankaj seems uneasy and confused, torn between trusting Sir completely and a new doubt that the break rule is unfair to Meena.

qa.q: What could Pankaj do instead of repeating "Sir said"?
qa.a: Pankaj could tell Sir about the stolen pencil box and ask whether Meena can play; asking is still respectful.

qa.q: What is break time like for Meena?
qa.a: Meena sits alone with her head on the desk, likely feeling sad and left out for something that was not really her fault.

grounding: Shows a child who follows a teacher's orders simply because the teacher gave them, not yet separating a fair rule from an unfair one.

"Pooja. Come here." Abhinav from Class 7 leaned on the railing, Sunny grinning beside him. "Kiran's tiffin is in the blue bag. Hide it behind the water tank before lunch."
"Why?"
"Because I'm telling you. Seniors' orders." Sunny laughed. "And not a word to anyone."
Pooja's stomach dropped. "Kiran didn't do anything."
"So? It's a joke."
At the lunch bell Pooja stood by the blue bag, hand hovering. Then she walked to the staffroom.
"Ma'am, a senior told me to hide Kiran's tiffin and not tell."
Ms D'Souza put down her pen. "Thank you for telling me. You did nothing wrong. Stay with me while I make sure Kiran has lunch, and I'll speak to Abhinav's class teacher before home time today."

qa.q: Where did Abhinav tell Pooja to hide Kiran's tiffin?
qa.a: Behind the water tank, before lunch.

qa.q: What was Pooja feeling as she stood by the blue bag with her hand hovering?
qa.a: Pooja felt torn and scared: a senior's order pulled one way, while a sinking feeling said it was wrong to hurt Kiran.

qa.q: What did Ms D'Souza's response get right?
qa.a: Ms D'Souza thanked Pooja, said Pooja did nothing wrong, kept Pooja close, looked after Kiran and acted on it the same day.

qa.q: What would have changed for Kiran if Pooja had obeyed?
qa.a: Kiran would have lost lunch and felt picked on for no reason, probably without ever knowing who did it.

grounding: Shows a child told by an older student to pick on a classmate and keep it secret, feeling the pull between obeying and a sense of wrongness.

Twenty minutes before the district final, rain drummed on the tin roof of the changing shed. Lakshmi's ankle throbbed from the morning semi.
Coach Wasim crouched beside her, voice low. "When the physio asks, say it's fine. The team needs you."
Lakshmi had looked up to him since she was twelve; he had taken her to her first trials on his own scooter. The word "no" didn't even form. She nodded, eyes on her laces. Ruchi and Anu, lacing up nearby, went quiet.
At the physio's table, Mrs Nair pressed the swollen joint. Lakshmi opened her mouth to say "fine" and winced instead. Mrs Nair looked from her face to the coach.
"She's not playing on this. I'm writing it in the report, and I'll call her mother from the stands now."
Coach Wasim walked out into the rain. Ruchi squeezed Lakshmi's hand.

qa.q: How long before the district final did Coach Wasim speak to Lakshmi?
qa.a: Twenty minutes before the district final.

qa.q: Why did Lakshmi nod instead of refusing?
qa.a: Lakshmi looked up to Coach Wasim and was afraid of letting him and the team down, so refusing felt impossible and she froze into agreement.

qa.q: What could Lakshmi say next time a respected adult asks her to hide pain?
qa.a: A short line like "I can't say that, it isn't true," and then tell a trusted adult such as a parent or the physio.

qa.q: What might it have been like for Ruchi to watch the coach and Lakshmi?
qa.a: Ruchi likely felt uneasy and unsure whether to speak up, which is why the team went quiet; the hand squeeze shows support once it was safe.

grounding: Shows a student pressured by a respected coach to hide an injury, freezing into compliance because refusing feels unthinkable, and an adult stepping in.

passage:
I'm Joseph, and I sit two rows behind Pooja in 11C, so I saw the whole thing.
Mr Sharma announced that the three of us who handed in the lab file late would get zero, no exceptions. Most of us stared at our desks.
Pooja raised her hand. Her voice shook a little. "Sir, I get why there's a deadline, and you've been fair with us all year. But the school printer was broken on Friday, and that's why we're late. I don't think a zero is fair here. Could we talk about it after class?"
The room went very still. Mr Sharma frowned, then said, "After class."
I don't know what they said. But on Monday the late files came back with a small penalty instead of zero. And Pooja still greeted him in the corridor, same as always.

qa.q: Why were the lab files late, according to Pooja?
qa.a: The school printer was broken on Friday.

qa.q: What does Pooja's shaking voice suggest about how she felt?
qa.a: She was probably nervous, because challenging a teacher in front of the class felt risky, yet she spoke up anyway.

qa.q: What made Pooja's disagreement respectful rather than rude?
qa.a: She said the deadline made sense, credited his fairness, gave a clear reason and asked to talk privately instead of arguing in public.

qa.q: How might Mr Sharma have seen Pooja's request?
qa.a: Because it came with respect and an offer to talk after class, Mr Sharma could reconsider without feeling challenged in front of everyone.

grounding: Shows a teenager telling a teacher that a rule seems unfair while staying respectful and asking to discuss it, separating respect for the person from agreement.
